Another McGinn corner from the right is met by Goretzka. This time, the German gets his header on target but it is easily saved by his compatriot Leno.

There is a VAR check for a possible penalty. Is there a handball from Berge in there immediately after Goretzka got his head on the ball? It appears that it did strike Berge’s hand and the referee is sent to the screen. We know how this normally goes...

That is a big early chance for Fulham which Iwobi wastes. Bobb steals possession deep inside his own half and drives forward into the Aston Villa half. Is that an example of the time of the game contributing to a decision? Goretzka is pulled back by Garcia, who avoids a yellow card. Had that not been inside the first few minutes of the game, it would not have been a surprise to have seen a yellow card.

With this being Aston Villa’s last home league game before Remembrance Sunday, Villa Park pauses to pay tribute to remember the fallen. Wreaths are laid in the middle of the centre circle before The Last Post is played.

As the pyrotechnics go off, both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are moments away from kick-off at Villa Park. Here is a reminder of how the two sides line up this evening:

Zion Suzuki had big gloves to fill this summer after the sale of Emiliano Martínez but already appears one of the Premier League signings of the summer.

Aston Villa’s new No 1 epitomises the vibrant energy of Unai Emery’s revamped squad and is a goalkeeper perfectly suited to the modern game.

The Japanese international is Villa’s own version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson, who revolutionised English football with a vast range of passing from his own penalty area.

Of all the daft statements to have come out of Aston Villa – and I am including Doug Ellis’s frequent claims that he invented the bicycle kick – it is hard to think of anything as absurd as suing a pundit for speaking the truth.

Jamie Carragher’s common-sense declaration that Villa manager Unai Emery might consider a move to Manchester United – because it is a bigger club – has apparently inflicted such a deep wound to the self-esteem of Nassef Sawiris, the chairman, that he has initiated a legal complaint.

Sawiris’s short statement, which he published on social media on Friday night, consisted of 37 ill-chosen words. It started by accusing Carragher of “unacceptable insults to the club and its fans”, then concluded with the vainglorious declaration that “Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football”.

Subs: Bizot, Harwood-Bellis, Mings, Barkley, Buendia, Garnacho, Mbaye, Joao Gomes, Madjo

Aston Villa manager, Unai Emery, is giving a full Premier League debut to Germany midfielder Leon Goretzka against Fulham this evening.

The 31-year-old joined Villa on a free transfer in the summer, but a knee injury prevented him from making an appearance off the bench until this month’s Champions League tie against Fenerbahce.

Asked what role Goretzka would have with Villa, Emery deadpanned: “The first one is to be available to play.”

Emery had also made a cryptic remark about Nicolas Jackson and Johann Manzambi in his Friday press conference. The suggestion was that they had been merely rested for Wednesday’s Carabao Cup defeat at Bournemouth.

But the Spaniard said: “For different reasons, not only rest.”

Whatever he meant is unclear, but both start for Villa tonight.

Fulham have won their last two league games – against Hull and Coventry.

Manager, Alvaro Arbeloa, has made one change with Sander Berge replacing Hugo Larsson in midfield.

Villa are aiming to win three successive league games for the first time in this calendar year. The omens are good as they’ve beaten Fulham in their last seven league meetings at Villa Park.

Tonight sees a battle between two Spaniards at Villa Park as Aston Villa host Fulham. Both sides are looking to bounce back from disappointing midweeks having been knocked out of the League Cup; Aston Villa lost 3-0 at Bournemouth, while Fulham fell to a 1-0 defeat at home against Crystal Palace.

After a slow start to the season in the league, Aston Villa’s form has picked up, which includes handing Manchester City their first defeat of the season a week ago. After this evening, Aston Villa have games against Barcelona and Manchester United before the international break but Unai Emery has insisted his full focus is on this game.

“If we are thinking after the match against Fulham, then we are making a mistake and we are completely wrong,” Emery said. “We are prioritising the Premier League, and this is the message. To keep our consistency and demands means that each match is a test.”

Having failed to win any of their first six league games, Fulham have now won back-to-back Premier League games, with consecutive 1-0 wins over Hull and Coventry, which has lifted them out of the relegation zone.

“It [managing in England] is a very tough challenge but I am so happy to be here,” Alvaro Arbeloa said. “I am where I want to be and I am really enjoying my days. I want to win games and I think we are performing well but we need to improve.

“They [Aston Villa] are very compact, they defend so well and even with the ball they know what they have to do. And they have top players, and when you have a top coach with top players, normally you have a top team. I think right now he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world. He is very, very good, he improves everything every year. It does not matter where he is coaching, he is doing an amazing job, and for me also it is a very good challenge to face him.”

In the two league meetings between these sides last season, it was one win apiece; Aston Villa won this fixture 3-1 just over a year ago before Fulham won 1-0 at Craven Cottage back in April. Team news from Villa Park to follow shortly.

#1098. Straight to work! Mauricio Pochettino lands in Manchester on a private jet to start work at Man United - with a vow that Man City's dominance of the city rivalry is 'gonna change'

Published: 02:49 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 08:00 EST, 18 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino made a promise to end Man City's dominance as Man United manager in his last interview as United States national team coach on Tuesday evening.

The new manager landed in Manchester at 11.32am on Wednesday as he prepares to start his new job later in the afternoon.

Pochettino had taken off from northern Kentucky in a private jet chartered by the club after his final match on American soil, which saw the US beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati.

But before becoming airborne, Pochettino had time for a final statement Stateside, after being taunted that 'Manchester is blue, and will always be blue' by one of his interviewers.

'No way,' he shook his head. 'You will see.'

'Give me time. Give me time and then that - that's going to change.'

New Man United manager Mauricio Pochettino made his way to Carrington straight after landing in Manchester

The Argentine took off from northern Kentucky in a private jet last night and landed at 11.32am

The manager shared a picture from his journey as he prepared to touch down at the airport (Source: Instagram/Mauricio Pochettino)

The plane believed to be carrying Pochettino and his staff was hired by Manchester United

Pochettino also shared a poignant farewell message to his US set-up, days after breaking down in tears in a press conference ahead of his penultimate time in charge.

Man United fans may also have been pleased to read of Pochettino's new-found love of John Denver's song Country Roads in his goodbye message, a song which is played before kick-off at Old Trafford.

'It is never easy to say goodbye, especially after everything we experienced together.' Pochettino captioned a carousel of photos of his time in the role. 'I always wanted the opportunity to coach in the USA, and I was very happy to have this chance with the national team. Two incredible years, with so many great moments and experiences that will stay with me always.

'From the challenges we faced at the Gold Cup to the excitement of the USA hosting the World Cup, and now finishing our time by reaching the semi-finals of the Nations League, I am proud of what we achieved.

'When we arrived, I wanted us to believe that we could compete with anyone. I hope today that belief is stronger, not only with the players but with everyone who supports this team. Not everything in football can be measured by results, and I believe we have helped build something important for the future of soccer in this country.

'This experience has re-energised me and given me so much, both in football and personally. I have discovered a wonderful country, made new friends and enjoyed so many of the traditions. Every time I hear Country Roads, I will forever think of all of you with a smile.

'Thank you to the players, staff, everyone at (the US national team) and all the supporters. Especially to those who believed in us and gave us this opportunity.

'Leaving is tough at this moment, but sometimes in football an opportunity comes that is impossible to say no to. I have always believed in following my heart, even when it means leaving a place where I have been very happy.

'I hope this team continues to grow and achieves all the success it deserves. Thank you USA.'

Pochettino had previously explained his emotions as stemming from how difficult the decision had been to leave the national team and re-start at Old Trafford.

‘I haven't prepared a speech, I'm talking with my heart,’ he said on Friday. ‘It's difficult for me to talk now because I am a very emotional guy.

‘When these moments arrive, it is always tough. Normally it is the opposite – you have been sacked! You cry because you want to stay.

‘I think it was one of the most difficult decisions of our career, but you have to move forward.

‘Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives.

‘In some part it’s a very sad decision, in another part we are professional and we are trying to make our dreams come true. We are excited for that step forward.'

Man United first made contact with Pochettino following their breathless 4-4 draw against Aston Villa in their last match before the international break.

The Man United hierarchy had previously given former head coach Michael Carrick a stay of execution amid a worrying start to the season, but as they prepared to head into the two-week pause in the relegation zone, the board became keen to make a change.

An agonising wait for Carrick followed, with the club legend taking training for multiple sessions at the start of the week as his future was openly mulled by executives including CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox.

After the duo returned from Monaco, where they had flown to speak to co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe about Carrick's future, the 45-year-old was finally despatched last Thursday morning.

Pochettino's United States farewell match went off in pitch-perfect style, which allowed thoughts to quickly move to the next task at hand after the final whistle.

Christian Pulisic helped make sure that Pochettino's reign in charge ended on a high note

The manager will now focus his attentions on getting Man United out of the relegation zone

'When you finish the game, you start in your mind to think about different things,' Pochettino said after the win. 'Of course, it's tough because it's emotional. Because I really love these guys, and I love the players. I love the staff. I love the fans and everything.'

Travelling with Pochettino were outgoing USMNT first-team coach Miguel D'Agostino, strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya and analyst Alec Scott, while his assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez as well as Pochettino's son and fitness coach Sebastiano have already begun preparing for Sunday's matchup with Liverpool at Anfield.

Man United paid a staggering £10million to cleave Pochettino and his staff away from the United States, after the head coach signed a new contract with the national team in the wake of this summer's World Cup.

The quick turnaround means Pochettino will be able to work with the players as they begin reporting back from international duty. Furthermore, he is expected to speak to club media before conducting his pre-match press conference around lunchtime on Friday.

Before boarding his flight, Pochettino not only waved to his adoring fans, but took a photo with staff and players on the pitch in Cincinnati.

'It's impossible not to cry, but that is because we care about the people and the people care about us,' he told reporters. 'When that happens, it's normal to show your emotions, no? Because we are human. We are no robots.'

#1096. Is the sixth great extinction imminent? Scientists must draw on natural history for clues

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Elizabeth Blackmore is in the Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut.

C. Brandon Ogbunugafor is in the Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut, and at the Santa Fe Institute in New Mexico.

Human activities such as hunting and agriculture have put pressure on populations of Sumatran orangutans, which are now critically endangered. Credit: Getty

The Last Animal: Human History and the Fate of Life on Earth from the Ice Age to the Sixth Extinction Kyle Harper Princeton Univ. Press (2026)

In The Last Animal, historian Kyle Harper asks a provocative question: how have humans affected animal biodiversity?

Explorations of species loss driven by humans are nothing new. But other books tend to focus either on the present day or on prehistory — the extinction of ice-age animals such as woolly mammoths and dire wolves, for instance. The Last Animal offers a continuous account of biodiversity from prehistoric times to the present day.

What does the future hold for the thawing Arctic?

What does the future hold for the thawing Arctic?

Assembling a historical account on this scale is a Herculean task. But, Harper argues, it is only by zooming out that people can appreciate how slow changes in humanity’s relationship with other species have led to the current biodiversity crisis. Humans have been reshaping animal communities for millennia, long before written records of extinction existed. By reflecting on how humanity got here, he contends, we give ourselves the best chance of turning things around.

The book is a triumphant piece of scholarship, both rigorous and engaging. And Harper’s ability to draw on ecology, Earth science and environmental history is impressive. At the same time, the book reveals limitations in previous research approaches. And it highlights how a lack of crosstalk between research fields prevents scholars from seeing the full picture.

Harper begins by discussing the spread of ancient humans across the world, starting with the emergence of Homo erectus nearly two million years ago. Human dispersal coincides with a marked disappearance of large animals from the fossil record. The reasons for this are uncertain. Some scientists point to climate change, but Harper suspects human hunting activity. There is strong evidence that humans were involved in the extinction of many turtle species, for example, which must have been easy and delicious prey for hungry hunters.

Humans were shaping animal life long before the dawn of farming, Harper notes. Mutually beneficial relationships with cattle, llamas and dogs, for instance, opened the door to domestication and selective breeding. And in Cyprus, prehistoric settlers intentionally introduced wild boar and fallow deer as game, permanently changing the island’s ecosystem.

Motorized vessels and industrial fishing practices have reshaped marine ecosystems.Credit: Getty

Later, deforestation and urbanization affected biodiversity. Since medieval times, commercial fishing has disrupted intricate marine food webs. And from the nineteenth century onwards, industrial farming, railways, refrigeration and pharmaceutical drugs have made it possible to raise vast numbers of cattle and battery hens in unnaturally good health, and in locations far from the cities that they eventually feed. These transformations in how humans live have had unintended and often surprising side effects on animal species. In the 1990s in India, for example, farmers gave the painkiller diclofenac to their ageing cattle, not realizing that it would remain in their systems and poison any vultures that fed on their carcasses. The birds experienced a sharp population decline as a result.

Writing about history with such a wide scope requires evidence from many disciplines. Harper’s chapters on prehistory lean heavily on fossils, archaeological finds and ancient DNA. Meanwhile, his historical chapters draw mainly on written records, including colonial accounts of animal extinctions that occurred as a result of European imperial expansion.

AI tools can design genomes. Will they upend how life evolves?

AI tools can design genomes. Will they upend how life evolves?

In part, this split reflects the fact that there are limited ways to learn about events that pre-date the invention of writing. But, Harper stresses, academic fields have also maintained somewhat arbitrary limitations on the time periods that they cover. For example, during the nineteenth century, when it became apparent that humans had existed for many millennia, historians decided to study only events that occurred after the advent of writing. They ceded “the murky time before written texts” to archaeologists, anthropologists and Earth scientists.

Yet, many changes in biodiversity span that boundary. Although the last woolly mammoths (Mammuthus primigenius) died out at the same time as Egyptian pharaohs ruled, their disappearance was part of a process that began during the Ice Age.

Even when extinctions are well documented, their causes and ecological consequences can remain difficult to disentangle. For instance, European arrival in, and later settlement of, the Mascarene Islands in the Indian Ocean during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries led to the loss of more than 50 animal species, including the dodo (Raphus cucullatus). Researchers don’t know to what extent introduced plants, animals and diseases contributed to these extinctions, or how colonial deforestation and hunting might have affected the island’s animals. These extinctions could be studied using a variety of scientific tools, from ecological modelling to ancient-genome analysis — but these opportunities have remained under-explored.

A few woolly mammoths survived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 4,000 years ago.Credit: David Zorrakino/Europa Press/Getty

#1095. Arsenal nous frustrates Liverpool as 14-year Anfield hoodoo ends with statement win

It is clear and obvious that Arsenal will be the team to beat in the Premier League title race, especially given that we do not yet know the fate of faltering Manchester City and their looming punishment.

A statement victory against Liverpool, their first in the league at Anfield since 2012, took Arsenal back to the top. And who would bet against them staying there and retaining their title?

Few would when they defend and manage a game – and it was game management in every sense – like this. From the formidable to the cynical – that was the statement. Against the Scousers, Arsenal had the nous.

“The mission was something we didn’t complete in 14 years,” Mikel Arteta said, having famously – in an Amazon documentary series – played You’ll Never Walk Alone to his players as they walked out to train to try and overcome a perceived mental block.

“There are reasons for that. Some of it psychological, some of it moments we did not nail on the pitch,” the Arsenal manager added of the winless run.

The result means that the north Londoners have already now won away at Villa Park, the Stadium of Light, the City Ground and Anfield. Stadiums where they dropped points last season. And that feels ominous.

A win would maybe have thrust Liverpool into the title race. Instead, under Andoni Iraola, and with an evolving young team – with promising 19-year-old midfielder Trey Nyoni handed his league debut – they are already nine points behind after just nine matches.

It is also clear, however, that they could have prevented this defeat having somehow been denied a first-half penalty after Alexander Isak’s shirt was blatantly pulled by Jurrien Timber as the striker tried to head home a cross.

Referee Andy Madley may have missed it, but what was the excuse of Stuart Attwell, the VAR? It was a stunningly poor decision – another bad day for Pro Ref and the use of technology.

It might be argued that Timber did not pull hard enough to prevent Isak from reaching the ball. But the defender grabbed the shirt and continued to hold it for a long time. It had to be a penalty. Little wonder Iraola said Isak should dive next time. Who can blame him?

What is also clear and obvious is that, once again, Arsenal’s resilience, defensive determination and appetite for toughing it out will be their greatest weapons. They are certainly, under Arteta, not here to win friends – just to win matches and trophies.

“That defensive line, that togetherness we have is undefeated. It’s something I have never seen before,” Declan Rice, who was also a stand-out performer and delivered a fine assist for the winner, said.

Arsenal’s version of the Yellow Wall was, indeed, hugely impressive – it is now six clean sheets from their nine league games and, despite all their pressure, Liverpool did not have a shot on target. That has never happened in the Premier League since such statistics started to be compiled in 2003 (422 games ago).

“That’s incredible. It did not feel like it on the pitch. Again, it’s the commitment of every single player,” Arteta said. And that was indisputable.

Even the expected second-half momentum, the expected surge of attack after attack as Liverpool faced the Kop, crashed on Arsenal’s back line. The visitors were so well-drilled that they stifled space – they refused to crumble.

Arsenal put their bodies on the line with blocks and tackles and a bit of time-wasting. There were dark arts, especially from both centre-halves with Gabriel going unpunished after claiming he was struck in the face by Isak early on – VAR anyone? – and the otherwise outstanding Ezri Konsa throwing himself to the ground after minimal contact from the Liverpool centre-forward.

In fairness there was also a bit of that from an increasingly frustrated Liverpool with Alexis Mac Allister going down after touching heads with Noni Madueke, having already tried to provoke Martin Odegaard with a hand to the head when the Arsenal captain was on the turf. That was not good from Mac Allister either.

And the only goal? Again, more frustration for Liverpool. It was well-constructed from Arsenal, but only after Alisson Becker’s loose goal kick, aimed towards Jérémy Jacquet, who was slow to react, was intercepted by Odegaard with Bruno Guimarães poking the ball to the right, where it was collected by Madueke.

There was an overlap by Rice and his low centre was precise and dangerous across the face of the six-yard area, with Virgil van Dijk unsure what to do. It ran beyond the far post where Kai Havertz side-footed home.

"Absolutely brilliant from Arsenal." Kai Havertz gives Arsenal an early lead at Anfield! ⚡️ https://t.co/eeyhRcLlel

After that? Liverpool swarmed over Arsenal, particularly in the first-half with Florian Wirtz’s free-kick cannoning back off the crossbar and Mac Allister somehow heading over. He was six yards out and unmarked, it was a glorious chance.

That was the hosts’ last tangible opportunity to score. As well as Arsenal defended, it was not a good afternoon for Liverpool’s forwards, Bradley Barcola in particular, although it was interesting to see Arsenal double-up on Rio Ngumoha when he came on. Arteta reacted by bringing on a second left-back, in Piero Hincapié.

Arsenal had the best chance with Alisson denying Christos Tzolis as the Greek winger’s low volley threatened to arc around him.

For Liverpool it became frantic. They could not surf the emotion, not against this battle-hardened Arsenal.

Boos rang out at the end – signs of how Arsenal had frustrated Liverpool – as Arteta gained his first win at Anfield as a manager. He was in the last Arsenal team to win here as a player 14 years ago. But this one meant more – that was also clear and obvious as he joyfully jumped into the arms of his assistant, Gabriel Heinze.

Here is a question I did not think I would be asking at any stage this season: will Liverpool win the Premier League?

It would be premature to describe this Sunday’s Anfield fixture as a title duel. Arsenal are better equipped to defend their crown, while Liverpool are a work in progress.

Whatever the outcome this weekend, Arsenal will leave Merseyside as the overwhelming favourites to claim back-to-back titles. They have a six-point lead over Liverpool. Should that extend to nine, Andoni Iraola’s primary objective coming into this season will remain unchanged; qualifying for the Champions League will represent a promising start to his reign.

What makes this weekend more significant is the champions will find a different Anfield to that which ended last season in such a downbeat mood, and came into this one uncertain of what was in store.

The discussion about what is achievable for Liverpool in the coming months is evolving by the week, the team bubbling along slightly under the radar.

There are several reasons why there are those who believe Iraola’s side might push Arsenal closer than anticipated.

#1093. Premier League identify FIVE key refereeing errors in one weekend as boss Howard Webb prepares to appear in front of clubs after Arsenal blunder

Published: 06:08 EST, 18 November 2026 | Updated: 09:16 EST, 18 November 2026

The Premier League have ruled that referees made five incorrect decisions in the latest round of matches as officials endured their worst weekend of the season so far.

It was unanimously ruled that referee Farai Hallam should have awarded Kai Havertz a penalty after he was tugged in the area during Arsenal's victory over Hull City, despite being in an offside position.

That is because the laws state that if a foul occurs before an offside offence, a penalty should be awarded.

Although Havertz was in an offside position, he had not committed an offence as he had neither played the ball nor interfered with play.

The key match incidents panel (KMI) said: 'Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded.'

Farai Hallam's decision not to award Kai Havertz a penalty was deemed incorrect by the key match incidents panel

Coventry were wrongly denied a spot-kick in their defeat to Everton after James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi's hair

1. Everton vs Coventry City: Frank Lampard's side should have been awarded a penalty when James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi's hair.

2. Arsenal vs Hull City: Kai Havertz was denied a penalty after being dragged down. The referee did not award a spot-kick because Havertz in an offside position. However, that decision was incorrect, as he was not committing an offside offence and a spot-kick should therefore have been awarded.

3. Crystal Palace vs Liverpool: Palace were awarded a penalty in the last minute of their 3-1 defeat to Liverpool after Milos Kerkez and Dario Osario clashed heads in the penalty area. The panel saw this as a natural coming together.

4. Ipswich Town vs Bournemouth: A penalty was given after Abdoul Ouattara tumbled over. The referee gave a foul against Lewis Cook despite Ouattara stepping across him.

5. Ipswich Town vs Bournemouth: Marcus Tavernier should have seen a second yellow card for time-wasting.

They did, however, praise the VAR for asking the referee to review the incident on the monitor despite Hallam's decision to stick with his on-field call after watching it back.

In the same weekend, Tottenham Hotspur complained to Pro Ref after Jayden Bogle's heavy challenge on Mathys Tel's ankle - which forced him off injured.

Spurs felt Bogle should have seen red, particularly after Crystal Palace's Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off for a similar incident in the week prior.

Reviewing the decision, the KMI panel were split but eventually concluded that the foul lacked 'the speed, force or intensity' to be considered serious foul play.

Two of the five panellists, however, felt that the challenge merited a red card.

Meanwhile, Crystal Palace's consolation penalty in the 92nd minute of their 3-1 defeat to Liverpool should never have been awarded.

The KMI panel unanimously agreed that the referee was wrong to award a penalty when Milos Kerkez and Dario Osorio clashed heads when contesting the ball, with the contact inevitable given both players were jumping.

However, VAR's decision not to intervene was supported because it was not a 'clear and obvious error'.

It is the second penalty incident in as many weeks that the went against Liverpool after Alexander Isak was wrongfully denied a spot-kick against Arsenal.

On the opposite side of Merseyside, James Tarkowski was fortunate not to concede a penalty for pulling Caleb Yirenkyi's hair during Everton's win over Coventry City, with the score still 0-0 at the time.

The panel found that Coventry should have been awarded a penalty and Tarkowski should have received a yellow card.

Last season, that incident would likely have resulted in a straight red card. However, the guidance changed this term with red cards only brandished if there is excessive force.

There were also two incorrect decisions in Bournemouth's victory over Ipswich Town.

Bournemouth defender Marcus Tavernier should have been sent off for a second yellow card in the 96th minute for delaying the restart during their 2-1 win, the panel found. However, it was a close call as the panel voted 3-2 against the decision.

Ipswich's scored penalty was also deemed to have been wrongly awarded, with Abdoul Ouattara stepping across Lewis Cook to win the spot-kick rather than being fouled by the defender.

The KMI panel consists of a representative from the Premier League and ProRef alongside three former managers or players and meets after every round of Premier League matches to evaluate significant refereeing decisions.

Ref boss Howard Webb will speak to Premier League clubs at a routine meeting on Thursday

While the panel is not new, this is the first season their findings have been publicly released in Pro Ref's drive for greater transparency and accountability.

Pro Ref boss Howard Webb is due to appear in front of clubs on Thursday at a routine Premier League meeting.

And in more positive news for Webb, he will be able to share that VAR delays are down this season after increasing the bar for interventions.

Meanwhile, the KMI panel have assessed 296 decisions this season - only six of which have been judged to be wrong post-VAR.

#1092. From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes.

But as Americans vote in the US midterm elections, it's time to think about how disgust shapes our politics, or whether our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.

"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.

But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale, developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.

"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."

Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.

"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.

Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.

A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.

However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.

Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.

Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.

"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.

Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.

"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."

The researchers surveyed 632 US adults, asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."

They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.

But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.

What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.

Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.

He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.

Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.

"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.

The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.

Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."

Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.

"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.

Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.

"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.

Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.

"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."

Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.

He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.

"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said. Edited by: Rosalie Delaney

#1091. Inside Midtjylland, the data-driven outsiders taking on Danish football’s traditional giants

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

Only formed in 1999, the club have used innovative thinking to become perennial title contenders – FFT headed to see them host rivals FC Copenhagen

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Beneath gathering rain clouds and surrounded by thousands of hectares of windswept heathland, FourFourTwo is staring at a 33-foot statue of Vladimir Lenin.

We're not in St Petersburg or Minsk – or any former Soviet nation, for that matter – but Denmark's Jutland peninsula, as it begins to drizzle with rain. It's so wild and remote that old Vlad is one of the few faces we've seen since arriving this morning. Much like the Russian revolutionary – carved in bronze, suspended in mid-air and lying flat on his back, just like at his Moscow mausoleum – we're beginning to wonder what the hell we're doing here.

“We like to imagine that Lenin is contemplating all the terrible things he did in life,” explains Birgitte Damgaard, the proprietor of the land the statue now calls home. Birgitte's father, a local textiles tycoon and art collector, vowed to rescue the statue after watching television footage of it being toppled by Latvians during the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. “It was brought more than 500 miles – first by truck, then by ship,” she tells FFT, after we stop by for a look. “He's been lying here, staring up at the sky, for more than 30 years.”

We're a few miles outside the town of Herning, although our own reasons for being here are more straightforward – we've come to witness a football match between local side Midtjylland and league leaders FC Copenhagen. At first glance, you'd be forgiven for thinking this is a complete mismatch.

From the capital, Copenhagen are Denmark's most successful club, with a record 16 league titles. Midtjylland, meanwhile, were only founded in 1999 following the merger of two second-tier rivals, and hail from a town with fewer than 60,000 inhabitants.

Yet the latter have rapidly grown into one of the country's most formidable sides, claiming four league titles in the past 12 seasons. Last term they won the Danish Cup, and beat both Celtic and Nottingham Forest in the Europa League. When we arrive, they trail only Copenhagen in the domestic league, heading into their table-topping clash. How have they managed it all?

We wave goodbye to Lenin and Birgitte in search of answers, driving through eerily quiet farmland outside Herning, to what appears to be a bunker from 007 adventure GoldenEye. Grey and austere, the building doesn't instantly strike you as welcoming – it turns out we couldn't be more wrong.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“We call this club the miracle from out of nowhere,” beams Midtjylland's bespectacled chairman Claus Steinlein, who shakes our hand enthusiastically before welcoming us into the warmth of the club's Dream 99 training complex. “Allow us to show you why.”

Opened in 2023, Dream 99 boasts a network of pristine football pitches, as well as a spa and gym. Steinlein leads us to a mural depicting the history of the club; a collage of black and white photos resembling newspaper cutouts. It's time for a history lesson.

“Midtjylland were formed from a merger between Herning Fremad and IFS,” he explains, pointing out a photo of the day the clubs came together – the suited, smiling chairmen shaking hands. “The name honours the Jutland province.” Indeed, Midtjylland means ‘Mid-Jutland' in Danish.

“We vowed from the start to become the biggest club in Denmark,” Steinlein adds. “People told us we were crazy. We knew that if we were to prove them wrong, we'd have to be different.”

Steinlein himself saw a way to help the new club stand out. “At that time, no Danish club had its own academy,” he says. “At least not with dedicated programmes. I wanted to be the first.”

Steinlein visited the academy of French side Nantes to learn what he could, returning with a blueprint for success. He asked the board to invest a massive chunk of its fledgling budget – around €800,000 – and, to his initial shock, they agreed. There was just one problem.

“Nobody wanted to send their kids here,” laughs Steinlein. “Children here grow up wanting to play for Brondby or Copenhagen, rather than Midtjylland. Convincing people was the first battle.”

A breakthrough came via Midtjylland's own kit man, who agreed to bring his 12-year-old son with him when taking the job. “It helped that his son was Simon Kjaer,” Steinlein says. “Simon went on to make more than 100 appearances for Denmark.”

Kjaer made a handful of first-team showings after graduating from the academy in 2007, before being sold to Palermo for €4m – a huge sum for a young Dane at the time. Steinlein's academy received a huge financial and reputational boost. “That gave our project the lift-off it needed,” he says.

Midtjylland began painstakingly forming partnerships across the region, more than 100 amateur sides regularly sending their best and brightest for trials. In exchange, Midtjylland provide equipment and tickets to first-team games. “It's about inspiring the next generation,” adds Steinlein.

Neither are Midtjylland's operations limited to the best Danish talent. We're led into an office to meet Jonas Dal, who heads the club's Nigerian academy.

“Every year, more than seven million children are born in Nigeria, compared with about 50,000 here, so the pool of talent is naturally much larger,” says Dal, who was once held at gunpoint during a visit to Lagos, but plays a key role in the Midtjylland project. “We bring over the most promising players. We have to be patient with them, because the weather and culture in Denmark are all very new to them.”

Right on cue, we meet Rilwan Hassan, who joined Midtjylland from the Lagos academy in 2010, before spending close to a decade playing for the club. He's now a coach with the academy. “It was so cold,” he recalls of his arrival as a teen. “But it was a massive opportunity. I was going into the unknown, but I quickly found out that this club was striving to be the very best. Everybody was pulling in the same direction.”

Many of Midtjylland's academy products, either from Nigeria or closer to home, are lured to the club with the promise they'll be sold if a bigger side comes in for them. Indeed, selling players has become a key aspect of Midtjylland's model. “If Liverpool or Barcelona come in for one of our players, that's perfect,” says Steinlein. “It means they've performed well and we can profit. Everybody wins.”

Following their formation, Midtjylland were immediately promoted to the top flight, before cementing themselves as consistent top-five finishers. Yet while results and youth development were impressive, they were beginning to struggle financially. Player sales barely covered the growing cost of operations, especially with European qualification hardly guaranteed each season.

“We'd wanted to become the biggest and best team in Denmark, but we were still some way off that,” winces Steinlein. “That soon changed, though.” The man who would help them take that next step was an Englishman with a physics degree, already making a name for himself at Brentford.

In June 2012, Matthew Benham had taken control of the Bees, then in League One, having made millions as the impresario of Smartodds – a company providing statistical analysis on sporting events to professional gamblers. That data also gave Benham extraordinary insight into how football games are won and lost, where and how goals are most often scored, and which players were being undervalued by the market. In short, a recipe for success.

That same year also saw Benham invite a Danish author to give a presentation to his staff. Benham had become fascinated by Rasmus Ankersen's book The Gold Mine Effect, which looked into cultural anomalies, such as why Jamaica consistently produces the best sprinters. Ankersen was equally impressed with Benham.

“At the time, Brentford were third in League One, and there were a couple of games to go,” the Dane would later recall. “I said to him, ‘What are the chances of you guys getting promoted?' When you ask that question, you expect an emotional yes or no, but he just said, ‘There's a 42.3 per cent chance.' That was when I knew he was a guy who was thinking very differently.”

Benham and Ankersen, the latter a promising player at Midtjylland before injury sent him down a different path, became firm friends. In 2014, the Dane convinced the data guru to invest in a second football club, with Benham paying £6.2m for a majority stake in Midtjylland. He brought with him his legion of statisticians, sports scientists and coaches. It was about to go turbo.

“This club now has tools to evaluate teams and players with much more accuracy using data,” said Ankersen, who was swiftly installed as chairman by Benham. “The model we're using could be applied in any country.”

Midtjylland's strategy was transformed overnight. “Set-pieces then became a fundamental part of the way we played,” Steinlein tells us on the balcony of the training complex, which overlooks the first-team's pitches. “They still are. We boast one of the tallest teams in Europe. We hire the best set-piece coaches and, when it comes to scouting, things like long-throws are key attributes. The approach has been successful.”

In Benham's first year, Midtjylland were crowned Danish champions; their first major trophy. The team finished with a goal difference of plus 15 from set-pieces. “We were finally the best club in Denmark,” grins Steinlein. “A dream come true. Benham's stats and our focus on set-pieces were key.”

We boast one of the tallest teams in Europe. We hire the best set-piece coaches and, when it comes to scouting, things like long-throws are key attributes

Next, Steinlein leads us into the main communal area of Dream 99. Above the only coffee machine in the building, where footfall is at its highest, a chart denoting Midtjylland's historical success from set-pieces adorns the wall. The 2015, 2018, 2020, 2024 and 2025 campaigns are highlighted as being particularly prolific – the Wolves won the league four out of five of those years.

“That one time we didn't win the title still bothers us,” laughs Steinlein. “We want our players and staff to be hurt by that, too. Topping this chart needs to be their motivation.”

Benham sold his stake in Midtjylland in 2023 to better focus on Brentford, though the two sides retain a close partnership. Today the club is owned by fashion tycoon Anders Holch Povlsen, Denmark's richest person, with an estimated worth of more than £12bn.

Ankersen has also departed, though his influence is still felt. A school called Guldminen, named after his book, was built into the Dream 99 complex. It aims to nurture both the best young sporting and academic talent in Denmark. FFT learns that students are given free rein of the building, meaning it isn't unusual for first-team players and schoolkids to share meals.

“We have a word for the environment we've fostered here: ‘sammenhold,'” says Steinlein. “It literally translates to ‘unity club', but it means so much more than that. It's about every person, from the kids to the first-teamers, coaches and cleaners, feeling part of something bigger. We are one entity. That's what sammenhold is, and it's our way of life.”

Overwhelmed by the scale and passion behind the Midtjylland project, FFT waves goodbye to the dream factory and makes our way over to the MCH Arena for tonight's crucial showdown against FC Copenhagen.

Inside the 12,000-capacity stadium, opened in 2004, FFT catch up with fans who are noisily drinking beer out of plastic cups and watching Brondby's early fixture on a big screen. Ahead of kick-off, we chat to lifelong Midtjylland fan Thomas Schouv Jacobsen. “My father is from Ikast, one of the two clubs that merged into Midtjylland,” he says. “Supporting this club since the start has been an extraordinary ride. The jump from winning a few silver medals to actually taking our first ever title in 2015 was indescribable. Seeing my father's face when we scored the decisive goal in the decisive match against Copenhagen is something that I'll never forget.”

Midtjylland's record against title rivals Copenhagen is certainly impressive.

Going into this game, the latter have won just twice in their past 14 meetings, with Midtjylland winning seven. Tonight, however, there's a fear that the league leaders might be too strong, especially given that regular Midtjylland defenders Rasmus Kristensen, Magnus Jensen and Martin Erlic are all out injured.

“We've had terrible setbacks in defence this season,” Jacobsen laments. “But, come May, we should have a very good chance of taking the championship. I think we have the best squad and the ability to come out successful.”

FFT also catches a moment with a Copenhagen fan. “We're massively important to Danish football because we have the biggest fanbase and play European football every year,” says lifelong supporter Kevin Willendrup.

“We're the flagship club. Our games against Brondby are by far the biggest in Denmark. There isn't the same level of hatred between the Midtjylland and Copenhagen fanbases – they've become extremely good in a very short space of time. Along with us, they're favourites to win the league every season. It's great that another team has emerged with so much quality.”

Yet there's no doubt in Willendrup's mind who'll emerge victorious tonight. “Copenhagen will win here for the first time in a long time,” he says. “We're on an incredible run under Bo Svensson and we're starting to look like a championship-winning team.”

As fans around us drain their beers and head inside, FFT does the same. We emerge onto the terraces to a magnificent sight. It's a record crowd, as flags swirl from the melee behind either end of the field. To our right, the home fans bellow into the evening sky and beat war drums. Off to our left, the white-clad Copenhagen fans are making their own thunderous racket.

Pitchside for the warm-ups, we see some familiar faces, including former Bournemouth beanpole Philip Billing, now at Midtjylland, and the ex-Cardiff targetman Andreas Cornelius, who is among the visitors' line-up. Curiously, Midtjylland's warm-up routine involves pain-staking set-piece practice; coaches repeatedly whipping vicious free-kicks into a packed box of giants.

As the players head inside to make their final preparations, we brush past former Everton and Real Madrid hard man Thomas Gravesen, who has presumably been loaned to a Danish TV outlet by the poker tables of Las Vegas. “Should be a good night tonight, guys,” he winks. “This is one of the biggest games of the season.”

The players emerge before kick-off to a deafening roar – the tifos, flags and rhythmic beating of drums providing an epic backdrop – before getting the game underway beneath the floodlights.

Copenhagen swiftly take charge but their dominance doesn't last. In the 12th minute, Midtjylland win a free-kick high on the left, not far from the corner flag. As Billing fizzes it in, FFT remarks that it's silly he isn't in the box himself given his size. He quickly shows us what we know, planting a ball squarely on to the head of onrushing Nigerian forward Friday Etim, whose effort crashes into the net to make it 1-0. Recorded wolf howls are played over the PA system as the roof comes off the MCH Arena.

Copenhagen dust themselves down and settle back into their rhythm, knocking the ball around menacingly, but they're unable to find a way through as Midtjylland's makeshift defence, marshalled by the imperious Andreas Maxso, clear everything.

Such low-block defending inevitably leads to mistakes, however, and one arrives just after the break, as wing-back Kjell Watjen fells Copenhagen skipper Thomas Delaney just inside the penalty area. The referee points to the spot and former Southampton star Mohamed Elyounoussi slots in an equaliser. The Copenhagen fans go wild.

The visitors take their possession up a notch. Robert Silva slaloms down the left and into the Midtjylland box, but his cutback is prodded away before the rebound is fired wide. Surely it's just a matter of time before they score again.

Then the unthinkable happens for the league leaders in the 62nd minute. Under very little pressure, Copenhagen goalkeeper Diant Ramaj passes straight to opponent Etim, who rounds the shot-stopper and shapes to pull the trigger, only to find his path blocked by recovering defenders.

As an entire stadium holds its breath, Etim squares the ball to Denil Castillo, arriving in support. The Ecuadorian fires low and hard into the Copenhagen net, and Midtjylland are in the lead once more, courtesy of a horrific error. Clearly shaken, Copenhagen never recover their rhythm. When the final whistle blows half an hour later, it's pure ecstasy for the Wolves supporters.

FFT rush onto the field to join the Midtjylland players as they celebrate in front of the frenzied home end. Arm in arm, players and coaches bounce in front of the melee, as we grab a word with Billing. “It's amazing when a result like this comes off,” he yells above the bedlam, with a huge smile on his face.

“We knew they'd play nice football, but that we could win it with our set plays and our physicality. We had to cope with a lot of injuries today, so the fact we came out of this game with a win is massive for us.”

When the players are finally separated from their adoring public, we're invited to join them inside. The dressing room is packed as victorious manager Mike Tullberg delivers a rousing speech in front of players, board members, staff and children. This must be what Steinlein meant by sammenhold. “I'm proud of you today, guys,” he says, singling out Maxso and his fellow defenders for an extraordinary performance. “There's a long way to go but we've given our ambitions a huge boost.”

A post shared by FourFourTwo (@fourfourtwouk)

Castillo, scorer of the winning goal, is also singled out in surprising fashion by the boss. “You've recently surpassed 100 games for us and what a way to cap it off,” Tullberg enthuses. “You keep playing like that and you won't be here for another 100.”

The whole room then erupts into an obscure song – a tradition that also sees players dancing and banging their lockers to the beat (watch the video above). It's a joyous scene. Afterwards, we head into chairman Steinlein's personal office, resembling a wood-panelled smoking room. The likes of Kenny Dalglish and Louis van Gaal have been guests here before us.

Drinks begin flowing and, at some point, FFT is only vaguely aware that the night is coming to an end. When we finally head back out into the cold Scandinavian air, it's with a sense that we've witnessed something truly spectacular – a wonder from nowhere.

With this result, there are just two points between Denmark's leading sides – one of them a traditional giant from an illustrious European city, the other a motley crew of dreamers and disrupters who refuse to accept the status quo.

It's the sort of revolution Vladimir Lenin, now lying flat on his back on a rain-soaked heath in our rear-view mirror, might have approved of.

Ed is a staff writer at FourFourTwo, working across the magazine and website. A German speaker, he’s been working as a football reporter in Berlin since 2015, predominantly covering the Bundesliga and Germany's national team. Favourite FFT features include an exclusive interview with Jude Bellingham following the youngster’s move to Borussia Dortmund in 2020, a history of the Berlin Derby since the fall of the Wall and a celebration of Kevin Keegan’s playing career.

#1090. Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns

Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

“I have to take the responsibility,” he said. “We did not transfer the things we did in training. Hitting long balls all the time, that was not the plan. We were not brave enough to play short passes.

“As soon as the referee blew his whistle, the plan disappeared. We could feel the anger and the frustration, I felt it on the touchline. We are low on confidence and it shows.”

Newcastle looked listless, clueless and alarmingly devoid of belief in what they were being asked to do. They have the unmistakable whiff of a team in decline.

If they do not start playing a lot better, they will be worried about a relegation battle. It is four defeats in their last five games and the confidence in Jaissle to find solutions is fading. Rather than change what he is asking his team to do, he has doubled down on the formation and tactics.

Concerns have been creeping steadily upwards since August. There is a lack of confidence in the players, and worries about the quality of the eight new signings made over the summer.

In particular, there are serious misgivings about the implementation of the “vertical football” Jaissle has imported to the North East of England from the Austro-German Red Bull coaching school.

A night under the lights at St James’ Park should be a boisterous affair, but things went flat quickly. Newcastle, as they have tended to do this season, resorted to long balls punted forward. More often than not they were poorly directed – only 22 per cent were accurate over 98 minutes.

There was no fluency and no threat. The first groans were heard inside 15 minutes as another pass was hoisted harmlessly into the air. They grew more widespread and more frequent.

Everton, just as they had in their Carabao Cup win last week, looked comfortable. Recognising how easy it was to nullify Newcastle’s game plan, they offered an attacking threat of their own.

A rising shot from Merlin Röhl briefly had goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek worried. A free-kick into the Newcastle box caused panic. James Tarkowski won the first header, but Thierno Barry swung and missed with his left foot.

The groans began to turn into boos and whistles. Jaissle’s side could barely string more than two passes together. It felt precarious.

This is not an easy place to play football when the crowd airs its displeasure. As the first half limped on, there were players in black and white who looked like they could not handle the pressure.

It was a horrible game of football. With the last kick of the half, Everton should have taken the lead, Harrison Armstrong picked out Barry inside the box, but he made a mess of the finish. The referee’s whistle was accompanied by boos and a scream of “sort it out” from behind Jaissle’s technical area.

He did not follow those blunt instructions. Everton took the lead in such simple fashion and all Jaissle and his coaching staff could do was shake their heads at each other. Tyrique George was played in far too easily from a free-kick but his shot should have been saved by Hornicek. It was straight at the Czech, but it went through him and it left Barry with a tap in. Newcastle appealed for both a foul on Fabian Schar and an offside but got neither.

Thierno Barry puts Everton ahead after Tyrique George's shot isn't dealt with by Lukáš Horníček! 🔵 https://t.co/oRXsrwbOhz

Everton had the lead and it was so easy and straightforward. They waited for Newcastle to give the ball away and then broke at speed. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was superb and forced a fingertip save from Hornicek. From the resulting corner, Hornicek was needed again to keep out Jake O’Brien’s header.

Newcastle tried to gain some momentum and finally created a chance. Harvey Barnes curled a cross to the far post. It bounced awkwardly but Anthony Elanga somehow failed to bundle it across the line.

Incredibly proud of the team all the time because their effort is unquestionable. There is not a lot of them but they are doing a great job and hope it continues.

I do not think anyone enjoys playing the same team twice so quickly. So for us to win both is hugely important for us. We want to get back to the top end of the league, it is incredibly tight.”

We take it game by game but tonight feels good and we can look forward to Friday [against Coventry].”

There are a lot of boos at the sound of the final whistle. A lot of forlorn faces on the Newcastle players.

That is a huge interception from Schar. Rohl drives down Everton’s right and spots the run of Barry into the box. He sends in the cross but Schar slides in to intercept. But did he go through the back of Barry to get to the ball? The VAR checks and decides that Schar got the ball first. The more you look at the replays when you really slow them down it appears that Schar might have made contact with Barry’s leg before the ball but it probably is not definitive enough to overturn the original, on-field decision.

Newcastle want a penalty as Hall goes down under a challenge from Rohl but is there enough in that to give a penalty? Probably not as VAR checks and clears the incident. It was a delayed reaction from Hall, who if he had gone down immediately after the contact may have changed the VAR’s mind.

How have Newcastle not scored there? From the subsequent corner, Garner’s delivery goes beyond the back post and picks out the head of O’Brien, whose header nearly sneaks in at the near post but is denied by the arm of Hornicek.

Elanga’s cross from the right finds Willock in the penalty area. Willock probably takes too many touches with too many players crowded around him and he is unable to get a proper, dangerous shot away.

It would be no surprise to see Matthias Jaissle turn to his bench imminently. On Thursday in the cup, he made a triple change at the break.

Everton come close to a second. A cross is sent in by George from the right and comes all the way to the back post. Branthwaite has the advantage massively height wise over Hall and wins the header, forcing Hornicek into the save.

Everton can smell a second goal with Newcastle all over the place. The home fans were hoping for a reaction after half-time but it has not happened for the hosts, who have not been at the races all night.

David Moyes’ side squandered some chances in the first half but they take the lead early in the second. Everton take a free-kick inside the Newcastle half quickly before Dewsbury-Hall slides an incisive pass into the box to pick out the run of George. He opens up his body and gets his shot away but it is too close to Hornicek. The Newcastle goalkeeper should do so much better but lets it slip underneath him, allowing Barry to have a simple tap-in to put Everton in front.

VAR is going to take a look at two possible offsides with both George and Barry under the spotlight. The Newcastle fans will be hoping for a reprieve here. The first one is cleared and so is the second so the goal will stand. You cannot say that Everton do not deserve to be in front. The Newcastle players also felt that Barry had fouled Schar in the build-up but the officials do not agree.

Armstrong should probably put Everton in front with the last kick of the half but misses the target. That is the final act of the half and it remains goalless at St James’ Park. Some boos ring around the stadium as the players head off.

That is a good late chance in the half for Everton. Dewsbury-Hall clips a dangerous ball in from the left and picks out O’Brien at the back post but the defender cannot guide his header on target. That was whilst Hall was still off and Barnes was operating as a temporary left-back.

Hall has received some treatment to his back and is now back to his feet.

Hall has stayed down after Barry collided into the back of the Newcastle left-back going up for a header.

George is dispossessed inside his own half before Willock plays it forward to Joelinton. The Brazilian takes one touch before shooting from just outside the box but his effort flies wide of Pickford’s left post. Joelinton struck it powerfully but cut cross the ball too much.

Barnes cuts inside from the left and drives across the face of the penalty area. His shot is semi-blocked by Branthwaite and loops into the air towards his own goal. Pickford takes no risks and palms it over his own bar. Hall’s delivery is headed on by Burn but then cleared by Mykolenko.

Garner is the one to take it but his effort is blocked by the wall. He tried to beat Hornicek at his near post rather than go completely over the wall but the end of the wall still blocks it.

Barry is fouled by Burn just outside the Newcastle penalty area and the latter is the first player into the book tonight. Burn protests his innocence but replays show that the referee was 100% correct with his decision. Burn is a touch fortunate that it is just outside the box. Garner and Dewsbury-Hall are stood over this one...

I would say that the Newcastle fans have gone from frustrated to now quite annoyed with how their side has begun this game. Plenty of groans and moans inside St James’ Park; their only relief will be that they are not behind.

David Moyes will be desperate to see his side score and take advantage of Newcastle not being at the races. The frustration from the home fans continues to grow and this is Everton’s opportunity. You cannot imagine that Newcastle will be this poor throughout the game.

That is a glorious chance for Barry that he should really have taken. A free-kick is sent into the Newcastle box and Branthwaite wins the header. The ball falls to Barry who, from ten yards out, has a big chance to put Everton in front but instead it is more of an air shot. In fact, he ends up kicking Osula to gift Newcastle a free-kick.

Rohl has Everton’s first proper sighting of goal tonight but he wastes the opportunity from the right side of the box, failing to keep his shot down and sees it go over Hornicek’s bar.

We are seeing many of the same issues with Newcastle United’s so-called vertical football under Matthias Jaissle already this evening.

Aimless long balls to nobody hoisted forward. Long balls aimed at someone who fails to win the first header or challenge and possession is given back to Everton.

There have already been a few grumbles from the home crowd as William Osula is sent off on another forlorn chase of an over-hit pass in behind the Everton centre backs.

We are nearly 20 minutes into the game and Everton striker Barry is still yet to touch the ball.

Joelinton’s shot from the edge of the box is struck powerfully and is blocked by Tarkowski, going behind for Newcastle’s first corner of the night. Hall’s delivery beyond the back post finds Burn but his header from just a few yards out goes wide. Burn should really be hitting the target from so close to the goal.

We are just a quarter of an hour into this one but you can already sense some frustration from the home fans. Everton, despite being away from home, have settled well into this game.

To sum up the frustration from the home supporters, Dedic plays a dreadful long free-kick into the box that has far too much on it and goes behind.

Under the lights at home, you would assume Matthias Jaissle would have wanted a fast start from his side but that has not happened for the hosts.

Barnes is afforded space to cut inside from the left and, from the corner of the penalty area, clips a dangerous ball towards the far post. There is slightly too much on it and the ball goes behind for a goal-kick, although for a moment Pickford appeared to be panicking. That is the second time Barnes has been given too much space to cut inside and if Everton keep allowing that, you would imagine that they will eventually be punished.

The two starting XIs are fairly similar to the ones that started on Thursday night but the obvious difference between the League Cup tie and tonight’s Premier League encounter is the change of ground. How big an impact can the Newcastle fans have on the outcome of this one?

Unsurprisingly, former Sunderland goalkeeper Pickford is roundly booed by the home crowd upon his first touch.

Ahead of Remembrance Sunday this coming weekend, with this being Newcastle’s final home league game before then, St James’ Park pauses to remember all those who have given their lives to protect this country. The Last Post is played after St James’ Park falls silent.

Both sides emerge from the tunnel and we are just moments away from kick-off from St James’ Park. Here is a reminder of how the sides line up this evening:

Newcastle have got some really good players. It is a Premier League game, we know a lot about them, they know a lot about us. I do not think there are too many big surprises tonight.”

“We picked up on what we can do better [against Everton], this is something we focused on in training, really committed in the last few days so hopefully we can deliver today.”

On Anthony Elanga returning to the starting line-up:

“It is important now after he was out for a long time with an injury. Now he is improving a lot physically and also getting the feeling to play with the lads again. Therefore he deserves to start today and hopefully he can put his potential on the pitch.”

On Will Osula starting after an injury scare:

On what he is hoping for tonight to get the three points:

“Be clinical, ruthless in both boxes. Defend with everything you have and then be efficient and use every opportunity to score and then I think we will see a great result today.”

“That helps us for sure. The extra motivation and extra energy will be there from the stands and that is something that we can always count on here at home in our stadium.”

“Nothing more than what I am sure you have already heard so he is not in the team tonight.”

This was going to be a younger, more dynamic squad that would grow with the club as they looked to live up to the promise made by David Hopkinson, the chief executive, that they would be “consistently and credibly challenging” for top honours in England and Europe by 2030.

Having sold Bruno Guimarães (£73m), Sandro Tonali (£90m) and Anthony Gordon (£67m), Newcastle were able to spend roughly £262.9m on eight players to reinvigorate the squad as they once again talked about challenging for European qualification in Matthias Jaissle’s first season as manager.

Newcastle are 12th in the Premier League, but have had an inconsistent start and there are concerns that too many of these signings have failed to shine. Jaissle is leaning heavily on the players he inherited from Howe instead.

It is always worth remembering that you only get a true reading of the Premier League table after ten games so this is a pivotal moment for both Newcastle and Everton as they play their ninth match of the campaign.

For Newcastle, a win tonight would take them up to seventh, just two points behind Chelsea in fourth. Despite the heavy away defeats and unconvincing performances, that would be an impressive start for a new manager. Matthias Jaissle has already felt the full force of the contrasting emotions on Tyneside in his three months in charge but big questions hang over his team. In particular, the “vertical football” style he brought from the Red Bull coaching school in Germany.

A defeat tonight, coming so soon after the 3-1 defeat in the Carabao Cup to Everton, will intensify the criticism of his approach.  It would also suggest Newcastle, despite all their positive talk over the summer, are nothing more than a mid-table team who will be looking over their shoulders rather than upwards this season.

A win for Everton will have the same uplift for David Moyes at Everton, also taking them up to seventh in the table. Given all the problems attached to their summer recruitment - or rather the lack of it - Everton will have defied the grim pre-season predictions heading into the second international break. The table is starting to take shape and so are the narratives around every club.

Newcastle and Everton meet for the second time in matter of days as the Premier League weekend concludes in the north east at St James’ Park. These teams encountered each other on Thursday night in the League Cup, where Everton won 3-1 at the Hill Dickinson to progress to the quarter-finals in that competition.

Newcastle, who won 2-0 at Crystal Palace in their last league outing, come into this game in 12th, with the chance to rise to seventh with a victory tonight. Their boss Matthias Jaissle has called on his players to use the defeat against Everton on Thursday as fuel for tonight.

“Now it is about taking that frustration into motivation for Monday and having that approach for the rematch,” Jaissle said. “We take it as a long-term journey, and our approach is to make progress, to see improvements. Now it is time to learn fast out of the mistakes that we just did. [There are] other phases where we can already see that we improved and this is something we can count on, we can build on, the good part. But football is also in the end about results so you need to avoid these simple mistakes.”

Everton, who have not won in the league since a 1-0 victory over Ipswich back in September, begin the night in 14th but, like Newcastle, could rise to seventh with a win. There are just two points that separate Bournemouth in seventh and Everton in 14th. Despite getting the better of Newcastle the other night, Everton manager David Moyes has warned that game will count for nothing tonight.

“It is a different ball game,” Moyes said. “Go to St James’ Park, on a Monday evening, they will get a crowd up there, you always know you are up against it. But we will go with confidence. We have played Newcastle a couple of times this year and done well, so we have to try and continue it. But Newcastle have got some really, really good players and players you have to concern yourself about.”

Jack Grealish was left out of Everton’s squad for that League Cup victory because of an unauthorised absence from training and the 31-year-old is not expected to be involved tonight.

These sides were involved in a dramatic fixture on this ground last season. Everton claimed a 3-2 victory, with Thierno Barry earning them all three points in the 83rd minute, moments after Jacob Murphy had equalised for Newcastle. Team news from St James’ Park to follow shortly.
